questions.q: Why does data written inside a container disappear when that container is removed and a new one is started from the same image?
options: Docker automatically encrypts and discards container data after 24 hours
A new container always starts from the image's original filesystem -- the old container's writable layer is gone along with it
Images are read-only and cannot be used to start more than one container
Only `postgres` images lose data on restart; other images keep it
questions.explain: Each container gets its own writable layer on top of the image. Removing the container removes that layer -- a fresh container starts clean from the image again.

options: A folder inside the image itself, baked in at build time
Storage that Docker creates and manages independently of any single container's lifecycle
A temporary cache that is cleared every time Docker restarts
A naming convention for container names, unrelated to storage
questions.explain: A named volume exists outside any one container. Removing the container that used it doesn't remove the volume -- a new container can mount the same volume and see the same data.

questions.q: What does a bind mount do differently from a named volume?
options: It maps a specific path on the host machine directly into the container, instead of using Docker-managed storage
It only works with the `postgres` image
It deletes host files once the container stops
It requires creating the mount with `docker volume create` first
questions.explain: A bind mount points at an actual host filesystem path -- commonly used for mounting local source code into a container during development -- rather than storage Docker manages on its own.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of `--mount` over the shorter `-v` flag?
options: `--mount` is required for named volumes, while `-v` only works for bind mounts
`--mount` spells out every part (source, target, type) as explicit keys, which is harder to get wrong on a long command with several mounts
`--mount` runs faster than `-v` at container startup
`-v` cannot be used with the `postgres` image
questions.explain: Both flags do the same job. `--mount` trades brevity for explicitness, which pays off on commands mounting several volumes or bind mounts at once.

questions.q: What happens when you run `docker volume rm` on a volume a running container is still using?
options: It deletes the volume immediately, even from a running container
Docker refuses to remove it, as a safety rail against deleting data something still relies on
It silently detaches the volume from the container without deleting the data
It converts the named volume into a bind mount automatically
questions.explain: `docker volume rm` only succeeds on a volume with no container currently using it -- a deliberate guard against accidentally deleting live data.
